name: Mouth tape

lead: Mouth taping means placing a strip of gentle tape over the lips at night to keep the mouth closed and encourage nasal breathing. Social media credits it with better sleep, less snoring, fresher breath and less dry mouth, and some forums link it to a better jawline.

Sealing the lips sends air through the nose, which filters and humidifies it and may reduce dry mouth, and better sleep can mean a less puffy, fresher-looking face. A 2025 systematic review found ten studies with 213 patients, with two reporting significant improvement in sleep apnea markers. The reviews looked at sleep and breathing outcomes, not facial shape.

paras: Users apply a strip or porous patch across the lips just before sleep and peel it off in the morning, usually after starting with short trial runs while awake. People often pair it with nasal strips or saline rinses.

The main concerns are taping over nasal obstruction or undiagnosed sleep apnea, skin irritation and feeling suffocated. Clinicians advise that people with snoring, daytime sleepiness or blocked nasal airways be evaluated first. Claims of adult facial-bone change from breathing route are unsupported.

angle.text: Users tape their mouths at night to push nasal breathing, aiming for better sleep, fresher breath and a less puffy morning face. Reviews have examined sleep and snoring, and they did not assess facial shape.

lead: Mouth taping is the practice of placing a strip of tape, a porous patch or a similar adhesive over the lips during sleep to keep the mouth closed and encourage breathing through the nose. It spread widely through social media, where it has been credited with benefits ranging from better sleep, less snoring and fresher breath to improved immunity, dental health and energy.[1]

Published research is sparse. A 2025 systematic review located ten studies with 213 patients in total and found that two reported statistically significant improvement in sleep apnea markers, while others found no difference.[2] A scoping review found nine eligible studies and likewise noted that only two reported significant improvements in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) metrics.[1] Authors of these reviews and of accompanying commentaries have called for more rigorous trials and discussed safety questions, particularly for people with nasal obstruction or undiagnosed sleep-disordered breathing.[2][1][3][4][5]

In looksmaxxing contexts, mouth taping is sometimes linked to the idea that nasal breathing and a closed-mouth posture influence facial structure. The reviews cited here evaluated sleep and breathing outcomes and did not assess facial shape.
infobox: Adhesive tape or patch over the lips
Marketed as consumer products; research on safety is limited[2]
Small studies, mainly for sleep apnea markers

paras: Products range from household surgical tape to purpose-made strips and porous patches designed to sit over the lips. The practice is separate from medical uses of tape or chin straps in sleep clinics, although some clinical studies have used tape to test the effect of enforced nasal breathing.[2][6][7]

Mouth taping circulated on social media platforms. A scoping review analysed the first fifty eligible TikTok videos using the term and catalogued the claims made about benefits, along with the type of person presenting them.[1] A 2024 editorial in The Journal of Physiology and a JAMA Otolaryngology comment on regulation reflect clinicians' attention to the trend.[4][5] A letter in the British Dental Journal addressed the practice from a dental perspective.[3]

sections.h: How it is proposed to work
paras: Proponents say sealing the lips forces air through the nose, which filters, warms and humidifies it. A small randomized crossover experiment in eight healthy adults found that mouth-taped nasal breathing over two hours increased oral mucosal wetness, whereas mouth-only breathing with a nose clip nearly abolished it; the work also examined upper-airway lining liquid surface tension, which has been linked to sleep-disordered breathing severity.[7] A meta-analysis of studies of nasal obstruction found it was associated with a clinically significant rise in apnea-hypopnea index (about 13.8 events per hour), which proponents cite as a rationale for keeping the nasal route open, although the review itself concluded very little about mouth taping.[6]

A 2022 preliminary study in mouth-breathers with mild OSA tested mouth taping and reported OSA changes.[8] A later two-night home sleep test study of 71 participants examined mouth puffing and whether taping the mouth during sleep altered oxygen desaturation index.[9] The 2025 systematic review pooled ten studies of 213 patients: two showed significant improvement in markers such as the apnea-hypopnea index or oxygen desaturations, while others found no difference.[2] The 2026 meta-analysis narratively reviewed two taping studies and reported reductions in apnea-hypopnea index in mild OSA, but no meta-analysis was possible.[6]

In patients already using CPAP, a randomized crossover trial of 62 people with OSA found that silicone hypoallergenic mouth tape increased average CPAP use by about 52 minutes per day compared with no tape.[10] A 2009 randomized single-blind crossover study examined mouth taping at night and asthma control.[11]
None of the cited studies tested whether mouth taping changes adult facial or jaw structure.

The 2025 systematic review was framed around the safety and efficacy of taping in people with mouth breathing, sleep-disordered breathing or OSA.[2] Commentators have discussed the possibility of taping over a blocked nose or in someone with untreated sleep apnea, as well as skin irritation from adhesive.[2][4][5] Clinical authors recommend evaluation of persistent snoring, daytime sleepiness or nasal obstruction.[2][6]

A small body of human research exists. Two systematic reviews and a scoping review identified nine to ten eligible studies, two of which found significant improvements in OSA metrics.[2][1] A preliminary study in mouth-breathers with mild OSA[8] and a two-night home sleep study of 71 participants[9] tested taping directly. A randomized crossover trial in 62 CPAP users found longer nightly CPAP use with mouth tape.[10] A trial in eight healthy subjects measured mucosal wetness and airway lining liquid surface tension.[7] A randomized single-blind crossover study examined asthma control.[11] A meta-analysis of nasal obstruction found increased apnea-hypopnea index.[6] The reviewers describe the overall evidence as limited.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, mouth taping is discussed both as a way to promote nasal breathing and jaw development and, by some users, as a sleep aid only; T Nation posters mention it in the context of snoring and sleep.[12][13][14]
